passage: Bhavna, you asked how I knew to act when your neighbour's bride went quiet. I am Himani, and I was twenty-six when I noticed it in the flat next door. Kamla had been married four months. She stopped coming to the terrace, her phone was always with her mother-in-law, and once I heard her say, "I'll ask my father again." My stomach knotted. I did not knock on their door and accuse anyone. I brought her tea when her mother-in-law was out and simply said, "I'm here, and I won't judge." After three weeks she told me it was money her family was being pressed for. I said it was not her fault and gave her the number of a women's helpline, and I sat beside her while she called. The counsellor there listened for an hour. I kept visiting every week.

qa.q: How long had Kamla been married when Himani noticed the change?
qa.a: Kamla had been married four months.

qa.q: How did young Himani feel when she noticed Kamla going quiet?
qa.a: Himani was worried and uneasy. Himani's stomach knotted, though Himani stayed calm and did not accuse anyone.

qa.q: What choice did young Himani make instead of confronting the family?
qa.a: Himani brought Kamla tea when Kamla's mother-in-law was out and said there would be no judging, then kept visiting every week, so Kamla could open up in her own time.

qa.q: How might Kamla have felt when Himani said "I'm here, and I won't judge"?
qa.a: Probably relieved and a little safer. After three weeks Kamla shared the truth about the money her family was pressed for.

grounding: A neighbour notices a wife withdrawn, watched and pressed about money from her family, listens without judgement, keeps in touch and points her to a helpline.

passage: Akash had six minutes. Baljeet's mother-in-law had gone into the temple across the road, and Baljeet, whom he had known since college, stood at the stationery shop with her phone switched off and her eyes on the door. Over the last months she had stopped replying to messages. The one time he asked how she was, she said, "Money is tight for them, and my mother-in-law says my family owes a lot." Now he bought two pens so he'd look busy. "I won't ask anything," he said. "I'm not judging. My sister saved a helpline number for women, and here's mine, if you want to talk or just have tea." Baljeet slid the folded note into her bag. When the temple bell rang, she gave the smallest smile. Three days later a text arrived: "Thank you for the pens."

qa.q: How many minutes did Akash have?
qa.a: Akash had six minutes.

qa.q: What is Akash feeling as he buys two pens and talks to Baljeet?
qa.a: Akash is worried and careful. He buys pens to look busy, says he will not ask or judge, and keeps it short so Baljeet is not put at risk.

qa.q: Which choice by Akash kept the door open for Baljeet?
qa.a: He did not push for details or judge. He gave Baljeet a helpline number and his own number, and offered tea, so contact stayed possible.

qa.q: How might Baljeet feel when she reads the folded note later?
qa.a: Probably relieved and less alone. The small smile and the text "Thank you for the pens" suggest she felt safely noticed.

grounding: A friend sees a woman withdrawn, watched and blamed about money from her family, listens without judgement, keeps contact and points her to helpline support.

passage:
Dilnaz first noticed it on the stairs of their building in Kondhwa. The new bride in 4B, who used to wave, now kept her eyes on the steps. Her husband, Deepak, walked a little behind her, always.
In the vegetable market on Friday, the bride counted coins twice and whispered, "He checks every rupee. His mother says my family owes them."
Dilnaz, twenty-five, didn't push for more. She said, "I'm on the third floor. Come for tea anytime. Even for five minutes."
She did come, on Monday, while Deepak was at work. She cried into her cup and said her parents didn't know. Dilnaz listened without asking why she hadn't left. Before she went back upstairs, Dilnaz saved the women's helpline number in her phone under "Tailor," and with her permission called the bride's elder brother right then, while they both sat at the table.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz save the helpline number as?
qa.a: Dilnaz saved the women's helpline number in her phone under "Tailor."

qa.q: What was Dilnaz worried about after the market conversation?
qa.a: Dilnaz was worried that the bride was being watched and blamed over money, and felt concerned enough to offer a safe place for tea.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz do that helped?
qa.a: She listened without judging, kept contact open, saved a helpline number safely, and with permission called the bride's brother that same day.

qa.q: What is it like for the bride when Deepak walks behind her?
qa.a: She seems watched and withdrawn, keeping her eyes down, which suggests she feels controlled and alone.

grounding: A neighbour notices a young wife withdrawn, watched and blamed about money, listens without judgement and links her to a helpline and family support.

passage:
"Yamini, you've cancelled on me three times."
"Sorry, Rajni. It's just... busy."
"You used to talk for hours. Now you reply in one word. And you're checking the door."
"He doesn't like me going out. His mother says I should be saving, since my father 'gave nothing worth mentioning.'"
"Has he hurt you?"
"No. No. It's just the talk. Every day."
"Every day isn't 'just'."
"Please don't tell anyone. It'll make it worse."
"Okay, listen. I'm not going anywhere. I'm not judging you. But can I call your Amma with you, now, from my phone? You don't have to say everything. Just that you want her to visit."
"...Now?"
"Now. And I'm saving this helpline number in your phone as 'Rajni Office.' If it ever gets worse, you call it."
"Okay. Okay. Dial her."

qa.q: What name does Rajni save the helpline number under?
qa.a: Rajni saves it as 'Rajni Office.'

qa.q: What might Rajni have been worried about when she noticed Yamini checking the door?
qa.a: Rajni was worried that Yamini was being controlled and blamed at home, and felt anxious enough to ask directly whether she had been hurt.

qa.q: What does Rajni do that could help most?
qa.a: She stays calm, says she isn't judging, keeps the friendship open, saves a helpline number safely, and helps Yamini call her Amma that same day.

qa.q: How might Yamini feel when Rajni says, "Every day isn't 'just'"?
qa.a: Yamini might feel seen and a little shaken, because her friend refuses to treat daily taunts as normal.

grounding: A friend notices a young wife withdrawn and blamed about money, listens without judgement, keeps contact, and connects her to her family and a helpline.

passage:
Harleen Didi used to be the loudest at every family lunch. At Lohri this year, she sat in the corner and ate nothing. When I asked about her job, her husband answered for her: "She left it. Better for the house." When my aunt asked about her new flat, her mother-in-law said, "What flat? Her father couldn't even give a proper car."
I'm Gurpreet, and I've known Harleen Didi my whole life. I kept looking at her, and she kept looking at the floor.
I didn't know what to do, so I followed her to the washroom. I just said, "Didi, I'm here. You don't have to explain." She held my hand for a long time.
That evening I called her brother, Eshaan Veerji, and told him what I'd seen. He drove over the same night to take her for a long talk.

qa.q: What did the mother-in-law say about Harleen's father?
qa.a: She said, "Her father couldn't even give a proper car."

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling while watching Harleen Didi at Lohri?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt worried and helpless, seeing a once-loud cousin silent, being answered for and taunted about her father's gifts.

qa.q: Why was calling Eshaan Veerji that evening a good step?
qa.a: It brought in family support the same day, from someone who could act, rather than leaving Harleen alone with what Gurpreet had noticed.

qa.q: What might it have meant to Harleen when Gurpreet said she didn't have to explain?
qa.a: Harleen might have felt relieved and less alone, because someone noticed her pain without judging or demanding answers.

grounding: A relative notices a young woman withdrawn, spoken for and blamed about her family's gifts, and responds with quiet support and family help.

passage:
Supervisor's note, accounts team, Friday.
Over the last two months Deepika has changed. She used to eat lunch with the team; now she eats at her desk. Her phone rings almost every hour, and she steps out to answer, coming back red-eyed. On Tuesday I overheard her say, "I'll ask Papa again, please don't shout." She flinches when anyone jokes about weddings.
I did not want to pry, so I asked her to join me for tea in the canteen. I said I'd noticed she seemed low and that she could tell me anything or nothing. After a long silence she said her in-laws keep asking why her family hasn't sent more. I listened without advising. I told her it was not her fault. I wrote the women's helpline number on a sticky note, and offered to sit with her if she wanted to call her sister. She kept the note. I will check in every day.
Zubin

qa.q: What did Deepika say on the phone on Tuesday?
qa.a: "I'll ask Papa again, please don't shout."

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling while noticing the changes in Deepika?
qa.a: Zubin felt worried and concerned, seeing her withdraw, flinch and return red-eyed, but careful not to pry.

qa.q: What did Zubin do that could matter greatly?
qa.a: Zubin listened without judgement, told Deepika it was not her fault, gave the helpline number, offered to sit with her while she called her sister, and planned to keep in daily contact.

qa.q: How might Deepika have experienced the tea with Zubin?
qa.a: She was probably scared and ashamed at first, then a little relieved to be listened to without being judged.

grounding: It illustrates a bystander at work who notices a woman withdrawn and pressured about money from her family, listens and points to help.
